clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant metaphyseal dysplasia caused by heterozygous COL10A1 mutations affecting type X collagen in the hypertrophic zone of the growth plate.
Presents in early childhood soon after walking begins, with mild short stature, bowing of the legs (genu varum) and a waddling gait.
Radiographs show metaphyseal flaring, cupping and irregularity that are most marked at the proximal femur, producing coxa vara; the epiphyses and spine are characteristically spared.
Biochemistry is normal — calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase and vitamin D metabolites are unremarkable, which distinguishes it from rickets.
It is the commonest and mildest of the metaphyseal chondrodysplasias, and final adult height is usually only mildly reduced.
Metaphyseal changes tend to remodel and improve after growth-plate fusion at puberty.
The lower-limb bowing and coxa vara can closely mimic healing or hypophosphataemic rickets on imaging.
Family history is frequently positive with variable expressivity between affected relatives.
reference.pathophysiology: The disorder is caused by heterozygous mutations in COL10A1, which encodes the alpha-1 chain of type X collagen — a short-chain, network-forming collagen synthesised almost exclusively by hypertrophic chondrocytes in the growth plate. Most pathogenic variants cluster in the C-terminal NC1 trimerisation domain and act through misfolding, impaired trimer assembly and effective haploinsufficiency (in part via nonsense-mediated decay), triggering endoplasmic-reticulum stress in hypertrophic chondrocytes. This disrupts the orderly progression through the hypertrophic zone and endochondral ossification at the metaphysis, giving the metaphyseal flaring, cupping and coxa vara. Because the resting and proliferative zones and the epiphyseal cartilage do not depend on type X collagen, epiphyses and vertebral bodies are spared, and mineral homeostasis is entirely normal. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with variable expressivity.
additionalInvestigations: Skeletal survey with long-bone and pelvic radiographs documenting metaphyseal flaring and coxa vara
Serum calcium, phosphate and alkaline phosphatase to exclude rickets
Assessment of renal tubular phosphate handling if hypophosphataemic rickets is considered
COL10A1 sequencing or a skeletal dysplasia gene panel
Standing lower-limb alignment radiographs and serial height measurement
Three-generation pedigree and screening of relatives
redFlags: Progressive coxa vara with hip pain or deterioration of gait requiring orthopaedic review
Severe or markedly asymmetric bowing suggesting an alternative cause such as rickets or Blount disease
Disproportionate short stature or spinal involvement pointing to a different skeletal dysplasia
Any biochemical abnormality or fragility fracture, which should prompt reassessment of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally good; as the mildest metaphyseal dysplasia it produces only mild short stature, with spontaneous metaphyseal remodelling after growth-plate fusion. Persistent bowing or coxa vara occasionally requires corrective osteotomy.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the child as having rickets and giving vitamin D, when biochemistry is normal in Schmid disease.
Overlooking a positive family history of short stature and bow legs.
Attributing vertebral changes to Schmid disease, as spinal involvement instead suggests a spondylometaphyseal dysplasia.
Assuming bowing will always resolve spontaneously, when some children need surgical correction.
references: Paediatric skeletal dysplasia atlas and reference
Clinical review of the metaphyseal chondrodysplasias
management: No disease-specific drug therapy is needed; management is orthopaedic and supportive, reassuring families that the course is mild
Monitor lower-limb alignment and growth with serial standing radiographs and height measurement through childhood
Reserve corrective osteotomy for persistent or severe genu varum or coxa vara that fails to remodel
Distinguish from rickets so that unnecessary vitamin D and phosphate treatment is avoided, since calcium, phosphate and alkaline phosphatase are normal
Provide physiotherapy and simple analgesia for lower-limb pain and gait disturbance
Follow through paediatric orthopaedics and clinical genetics, anticipating spontaneous remodelling after growth-plate fusion
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal dominant COL10A1 disorder and assess affected relatives
